citations.quote: In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. The model also states explicitly the conditional-mean identity used below: $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_t]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$ for every such $B$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
Let $\mathcal H_{t-1}$ be the pre-round history sigma-algebra generated by the previously played choices and all previously revealed loss vectors (any random loss vector is assumed measurable on the protocol's probability space). The weights and $x_t$ are $\mathcal H_{t-1}$-measurable. Draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with conditional distribution
$$\mathbb P(I_t=i\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=x_t(i)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad i\in[N],$$
and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. Every factor $\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i))$ is a positive finite real; from the positive finite initial weights it follows by induction that every normalizing denominator is positive and finite. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let a finite-horizon online protocol have horizon $T$, action set $K$, round losses $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, and learner choices $x_t\in K$. Whenever a minimum below is used, assume it is finite and attained. For a fixed comparator $u\in K$, the realized regret is
$$
R_T(u):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
The **static regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm stat}:=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
For randomized learners or environments, **expected regret** is the expectation of the specified regret random variable over their joint randomness, when that random variable is measurable and integrable. In a stochastic finite-arm reward model with means $(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}$, let $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$. The **pseudo-regret** is the random variable
$$
\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}),
$$
whereas the **realized reward regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t).
$$

For dynamic comparators, suppose $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for a positive integer $d$ and fix a norm $\|\cdot\|:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$, meaning $\|v\|=0$ exactly when $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|$. Given a comparator sequence $u_{1:T}=(u_1,\ldots,u_T)\in K^T$, the **dynamic regret** and its **path length** are
$$
R_T^{\rm dyn}(u_{1:T}):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t),\qquad P(u_{1:T}):=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|u_t-u_{t+1}\|.
$$
For a nonempty contiguous integer interval $I=[r,s]$ with $1\le r\le s\le T$, its **interval regret** is
$$
R_I:=\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u),
$$
and the **adaptive regret** is $\max_{1\le r\le s\le T}R_{[r,s]}$. For an algorithm $A$ producing the choices $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, write $R_I(A)$ for its interval regret on $I$. The algorithm is **strongly adaptive** relative to a specified loss, feedback, adversary, and comparator class only if there are a stated base algorithm $A_0$, constants $C>0$ and $p\ge0$, and a specified bound $B_{A_0}(n)$ on $A_0$'s static regret at horizon $n$ in that same class, such that for every nonempty contiguous interval $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}$,
$$
R_I(A)\le C\bigl(\log(eT)\bigr)^p B_{A_0}(|I|),
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $|I|=s-r+1$. Strong adaptivity is a regret property relative to intervals; it does not imply anytime statistical validity.

Fix a positive integer horizon $T$, a nonempty action set $K$, and, when choices or the environment are randomized, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. An online decision protocol has rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$. Before round $t$, the learner has the history $h_{t-1}$ consisting of its earlier choices and all feedback and loss information revealed in earlier rounds. It chooses $x_t\in K$ using only $h_{t-1}$ and any learner-private randomization available by that time. In a randomized protocol, $X_t$ is a measurable random element of $K$, meaning a measurable map from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $K$ equipped with its declared measurable structure. The environment supplies a real-valued loss function $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$; it may have fixed $f_t$ before the choice or choose it after the choice, as specified by the environment model, but the learner does not observe $f_t$ before choosing $x_t$. The learner incurs loss $f_t(x_t)$ and then receives feedback about round $t$ according to the feedback model. The history $h_t$ adds $x_t$, the feedback received, and any part of $f_t$ explicitly revealed in round $t$. No convexity, boundedness, or regret guarantee is part of this protocol definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: For every $z\ge0$, [F2] gives $\exp(z)\ge1+z>0$, so [F3] gives $\exp(-z)\le1/(1+z)$. Since $(1-z+z^2)(1+z)=1+z^3\ge1$ and $1+z>0$, one also has $1/(1+z)\le1-z+z^2$. Thus $\exp(-z)\le1-z+z^2$ for all $z\ge0$.

Put $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^N W_t(i)$, $m_t=\sum_i x_t(i)\ell_t(i)$, and $q_t=\sum_i x_t(i)\ell_t(i)^2$. By [F1], all weights are positive finite by induction, so $S_t>0$ and $x_t$ is a probability vector. Applying step 1.1 to $z=\epsilon\ell_t(i)$ and summing with weights $x_t(i)$ gives $S_{t+1}=S_t\sum_i x_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i))\le S_t(1-\epsilon m_t+\epsilon^2q_t)\le S_t\exp(-\epsilon m_t+\epsilon^2q_t)$, where the last inequality is [F2].

Dividing the positive ratios from step 2.1 by $S_t$ and multiplying over $t$, then using [F4] and $S_1=N$, gives $S_{T+1}\le N\exp(-\epsilon\sum_t m_t+\epsilon^2\sum_t q_t)$. For any fixed $i^\star$, [F1] also gives $S_{T+1}\ge W_{T+1}(i^\star)=\exp(-\epsilon\sum_t\ell_t(i^\star))$. Since $N=\exp(\log N)$ by [F6], combining the bounds and applying [F5] yields $-\epsilon\sum_t\ell_t(i^\star)\le\log N-\epsilon\sum_t m_t+\epsilon^2\sum_t q_t$.
Rearranging step 3.1 and dividing by $\epsilon>0$ gives $\sum_t m_t\le\sum_t\ell_t(i^\star)+\epsilon\sum_tq_t+\log(N)/\epsilon$, which is the first assertion.

For losses in $[0,1]$, $q_t\le\sum_i x_t(i)=1$. Since $[N]$ is finite and nonempty, fix $i^\star$ attaining $\min_i\sum_t\ell_t(i)$. If $N\ge2$, then $N>1$ and [F7] gives $\log N>\log1=0$, so $\epsilon=\sqrt{\log N/T}$ is positive; step 4.1 now gives the deterministic mixed-loss regret bound $\epsilon T+\log N/\epsilon=2\sqrt{T\log N}$. If $N=1$, the only sampled expert is the only comparator, so the static regret is zero.

For each $t$, $\ell_t(I_t)=\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_t(i)\mathbf 1_{\{I_t=i\}}$. By [A1], the entire loss sequence is fixed before randomization; [F11] gives the choice-before-feedback order, and [F1] makes every $x_t$ deterministic from the fixed losses and previous updates. Thus [F8]–[F9] give $\mathbb E[\ell_t(I_t)]=\sum_i\ell_t(i)\mathbb P(I_t=i)=m_t$ and $\mathbb E[\sum_t\ell_t(I_t)]=\sum_t m_t$. The bounded losses are measurable by the algorithm's protocol and integrable by [F12]. Subtracting the deterministic best-expert loss proves the expected static-regret assertion from step 5.1 using [F10].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $x\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $K\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, with metric projection $P_K:H\to K$, the unique nearest point map of [[thm-projection-onto-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]. Then for all $x,y\in H$
$$\|P_Kx-P_Ky\|\le\|x-y\|,$$
and $P_K$ is firmly nonexpansive in the equivalent forms
$$\langle P_Kx-P_Ky,\,x-y\rangle\ge\|P_Kx-P_Ky\|^2,\qquad \langle (x-P_Kx)-(y-P_Ky),\,P_Kx-P_Ky\rangle\ge0 .$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

derivations.claim: If $D=0$, the diameter condition and nonemptiness make $K$ a singleton, so $x_t=u$ and every loss difference is zero. If $G=0$, then $g_t=0$ by the positive-definite Euclidean norm in [F1], and [F5] or [F6] gives $f_t(x_t)-f_t(u)\le0$ on each round; the sum is nonpositive. These branches use no projection and no choice axiom. Hence assume $D,G>0$.

By [A1], [F1], [F2], and the closedness of $K$ in the metric topology [F8], the nondegenerate algorithm has a unique projection at every update. If inputs are random, [F4] makes the projection continuous, so composition with the measurable vector operation $x_t-\eta_tg_t$ keeps $x_{t+1}$ measurable.

Fix $u\in K$, put $a_t=\|x_t-u\|_2^2$, $y_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tg_t$, and $x_{t+1}=P_K(y_{t+1})$. By [F3], $\langle y_{t+1}-x_{t+1},u-x_{t+1}\rangle\le0$, whence $\|y_{t+1}-u\|_2^2-\|x_{t+1}-u\|_2^2=\|y_{t+1}-x_{t+1}\|_2^2+2\langle y_{t+1}-x_{t+1},x_{t+1}-u\rangle\ge0$. Expanding $y_{t+1}$ therefore gives $a_{t+1}\le a_t-2\eta_t\langle g_t,x_t-u\rangle+\eta_t^2\|g_t\|_2^2$.

The stated domains are convex by [F9], and [F10] identifies the smooth-branch vector $g_t$ with the gradient in Euclidean coordinates. Thus in the smooth branch [F5] gives $f_t(x_t)-f_t(u)\le\langle g_t,x_t-u\rangle$; in the nonsmooth branch the same inequality is an explicit hypothesis in the Statement and follows from [F6]. Rearranging step 2.1 and using $\|g_t\|_2\le G$ yields $f_t(x_t)-f_t(u)\le(a_t-a_{t+1})/(2\eta_t)+\eta_tG^2/2$.

Since $x_t,u\in K$, the diameter hypothesis gives $0\le a_t\le D^2$ for every $t$, while $a_{T+1}\ge0$. Also $1/\eta_t=G\sqrt t/D$ is nondecreasing because $D,G>0$. Summing step 3.1 gives $\sum_{t=1}^T(f_t(x_t)-f_t(u))\le D^2/(2\eta_T)+(G^2/2)\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t$. The exact telescoping identity is $\sum_{t=1}^T(a_t-a_{t+1})/\eta_t=a_1/\eta_1+\sum_{t=2}^T a_t(1/\eta_t-1/\eta_{t-1})-a_{T+1}/\eta_T$. Every coefficient $1/\eta_t-1/\eta_{t-1}$ is nonnegative, so $a_t\le D^2$ and $a_{T+1}\ge0$ bound this by $D^2(1/\eta_1+\sum_{t=2}^T(1/\eta_t-1/\eta_{t-1}))=D^2/\eta_T$.

With $\eta_t=D/(G\sqrt t)$, the first term in step 4.1 is $DG\sqrt T/2$. For every integer $t\ge1$, $1/\sqrt t\le2(\sqrt t-\sqrt{t-1})$ because $\sqrt t+\sqrt{t-1}\le2\sqrt t$; summing telescopically gives $\sum_{t=1}^T1/\sqrt t\le2\sqrt T$. Thus the second term is at most $DG\sqrt T$, proving the pointwise comparator bound.

If the finite-horizon loss sum attains a finite minimum at $u^\star\in K$, substitute $u^\star$ into the bound just proved. The left side becomes the static regret of [F7], giving the stated static-regret consequence.

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
Let $\mathcal H_{t-1}$ be the pre-round history sigma-algebra generated by the previously played choices and all previously revealed loss vectors (any random loss vector is assumed measurable on the protocol's probability space). The weights and $x_t$ are $\mathcal H_{t-1}$-measurable. Draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with conditional distribution
$$\mathbb P(I_t=i\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=x_t(i)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad i\in[N],$$
and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. Every factor $\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i))$ is a positive finite real; from the positive finite initial weights it follows by induction that every normalizing denominator is positive and finite. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. The model also states explicitly the conditional-mean identity used below: $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_t]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$ for every such $B$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

Let a finite-horizon online protocol have horizon $T$, action set $K$, round losses $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, and learner choices $x_t\in K$. Whenever a minimum below is used, assume it is finite and attained. For a fixed comparator $u\in K$, the realized regret is
$$
R_T(u):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
The **static regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm stat}:=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
For randomized learners or environments, **expected regret** is the expectation of the specified regret random variable over their joint randomness, when that random variable is measurable and integrable. In a stochastic finite-arm reward model with means $(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}$, let $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$. The **pseudo-regret** is the random variable
$$
\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}),
$$
whereas the **realized reward regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t).
$$

For dynamic comparators, suppose $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for a positive integer $d$ and fix a norm $\|\cdot\|:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$, meaning $\|v\|=0$ exactly when $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|$. Given a comparator sequence $u_{1:T}=(u_1,\ldots,u_T)\in K^T$, the **dynamic regret** and its **path length** are
$$
R_T^{\rm dyn}(u_{1:T}):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t),\qquad P(u_{1:T}):=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|u_t-u_{t+1}\|.
$$
For a nonempty contiguous integer interval $I=[r,s]$ with $1\le r\le s\le T$, its **interval regret** is
$$
R_I:=\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u),
$$
and the **adaptive regret** is $\max_{1\le r\le s\le T}R_{[r,s]}$. For an algorithm $A$ producing the choices $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, write $R_I(A)$ for its interval regret on $I$. The algorithm is **strongly adaptive** relative to a specified loss, feedback, adversary, and comparator class only if there are a stated base algorithm $A_0$, constants $C>0$ and $p\ge0$, and a specified bound $B_{A_0}(n)$ on $A_0$'s static regret at horizon $n$ in that same class, such that for every nonempty contiguous interval $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}$,
$$
R_I(A)\le C\bigl(\log(eT)\bigr)^p B_{A_0}(|I|),
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $|I|=s-r+1$. Strong adaptivity is a regret property relative to intervals; it does not imply anytime statistical validity.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Fix a positive integer horizon $T$, a nonempty action set $K$, and, when choices or the environment are randomized, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. An online decision protocol has rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$. Before round $t$, the learner has the history $h_{t-1}$ consisting of its earlier choices and all feedback and loss information revealed in earlier rounds. It chooses $x_t\in K$ using only $h_{t-1}$ and any learner-private randomization available by that time. In a randomized protocol, $X_t$ is a measurable random element of $K$, meaning a measurable map from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $K$ equipped with its declared measurable structure. The environment supplies a real-valued loss function $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$; it may have fixed $f_t$ before the choice or choose it after the choice, as specified by the environment model, but the learner does not observe $f_t$ before choosing $x_t$. The learner incurs loss $f_t(x_t)$ and then receives feedback about round $t$ according to the feedback model. The history $h_t$ adds $x_t$, the feedback received, and any part of $f_t$ explicitly revealed in round $t$. No convexity, boundedness, or regret guarantee is part of this protocol definition.

routine_steps.claim: The learner chooses before round-one feedback by [F7]; the displayed loss vectors are fixed in advance by [F2]. Initially $x_1=(1/2,1/2)$. By [F5], the round-one update multiplies expert 2's weight by $1/2$ and expert 1's by $1$, giving $W_2=(1,1/2)$ and $x_2=(2/3,1/3)$.

The mixed losses are $\sum_i x_1(i)\ell_1(i)=1/2$ and $\sum_i x_2(i)\ell_2(i)=2/3$. By [F2], [F4], [F6], and the algorithm's measurable sampling in [F1], these are the expected sampled losses, so the expected cumulative loss is $7/6$.
Expert 1's total loss is $0+1=1$, and expert 2's is $1+0=1$. Hence the best fixed expert has loss $1$ and [F3] gives expected static regret $7/6-1=1/6$; the finite losses are integrable by [F6].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $x\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).$$

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].
